paragraphs.text: 1 Now it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus, (this is Ahasuerus which reigned, from India even unto Ethiopia, over an hundred and seven and twenty provinces:) 2 That in those days, when the king Ahasuerus sat on the throne of his kingdom, which was in Shushan the palace, 3 In the third year of his reign, he made a feast unto all his princes and his servants; the power of Persia and Media, the nobles and princes of the provinces, being before him: 4 When he shewed the riches of his glorious kingdom and the honour of his excellent majesty many days, even an hundred and fourscore days. 5 And when these days were expired, the king made a feast unto all the people that were present in Shushan the palace, both unto great and small, seven days, in the court of the garden of the king’s palace; 6 Where were white, green, and blue, hangings, fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings and pillars of marble: the beds were of gold and silver, upon a pavement of alabaster, and marble, and pearl, and black marble. 7 And they gave them drink in vessels of gold, (the vessels being diverse one from another,) and royal wine in abundance, according to the state of the king. 8 And the drinking was according to the law; none did compel: for so the king had appointed to all the officers of his house, that they should do according to every man’s pleasure. 9 Also Vashti the queen made a feast for the women in the royal house which belonged to king Ahasuerus.

The kingdom of Media and Persia grew great and defeated the kingdom of Babylon, so the Jews who had been carried captive to Babylon came under Persian rule. The extent of this kingdom reached the point that it contained 127 provinces (states) stretching from India to Cush [1], that is, to Nubia and Kordofan, south of Egypt and north of Ethiopia. Among these provinces was the province of Egypt, which the emperor Xerxes occupied after his father had failed to seize it.

We have said that Ahasuerus [1] means King Xerxes the son of Darius. Since more than one king was given the title Ahasuerus, some scholars see that this word does not signify the king’s name but is a title special to the kings of Persia, like saying “Pharaoh” of the king of Egypt.

The king wanted to show the riches of the glory of his kingdom and the honour of the splendor of his majesty [4], so he made two great feasts. The first lasted 180 days; perhaps he held a daily feast for each province separately, together with special feasts for the princes as a body, or perhaps these cities covered the long period of preparing the two feasts. As for the second feast, [it was held for all the people, from great to small, a feast of seven days in the court of the garden of the king’s palace] [5].
Perhaps he prepared these two feasts in order to devise the plan of war against Greece, for Herodotus says that the Persians were accustomed to take their decisions at such feasts.

The book describes the feast in precise detail, mentioning that it was held in Shushan the palace. “Shushan,” or “Susa,” has been the capital of Elam since about the year 3000 B.C.; it was the seat of King Chedorlaomer (Gen 14:1). The kings of Media and Persia took possession of it and made it a capital alongside Babylon and Ecbatana, and the kings preferred to stay in it, especially in the winter. The first feast, for the princes, was apparently held inside the palace. The second, which included all the people residing in the palace and its dependencies (it seems it was separate from the city itself (Esth 9:12-13)), was held in the garden of the palace, where there were hangings (fabrics) of white, green and blue, which are the royal colors in Persia. These hangings were fastened with cords of fine linen (white linen) and purple to rings of silver and pillars of marble; the hangings were used for protection from the heat of the sun. The beds were inlaid with gold and silver upon a pavement, that is, a floor of tiles, of alabaster (a white stone that gleams), marble, pearl and black marble. The most notable feature of the feast was the drinking of the royal wine, which was found in abundance “according to the state of the king” [7], but he left the freedom of drinking to the choice of each person.
At the time when the king held this feast, the queen also held a feast for the women in the king’s house.

10 On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king, 11 To bring Vashti the queen before the king with the crown royal, to shew the people and the princes her beauty: for she was fair to look on. 12 But the queen Vashti refused to come at the king’s commandment by his chamberlains: therefore was the king very wroth, and his anger burned in him.

“On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king, to bring Vashti the queen before the king with the crown royal, to shew the people and the princes her beauty: for she was fair to look on” [10-11].

The king’s heart was merry with wine, so he lost his balance, and in foolishness he asked his seven chamberlains to bring the queen so that her beauty might be shown to the peoples and the princes. Here the word “eunuch” (chamberlain) does not carry its literal meaning, that is, a castrated man, but is a title that was given to the holders of royal offices in Egypt and Persia. Potiphar, the captain of the guard, was called “an officer of Pharaoh” (Gen 39:1), and so were the chief of Pharaoh’s cupbearers and his chief baker (Gen 40:2)... So the seven chamberlains are the men entrusted with the royal affairs, and they enjoy the favor of servants before the king.

The king’s heart was merry with wine, so he uttered perverse things, as the wise man says: “Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright. At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder... thine heart shall utter perverse things” (Prov 23:31-33); “It is not for kings... to drink wine; nor for princes strong drink: lest they drink, and forget the law, and pervert the judgment of any of the afflicted” (Prov 31:4-5).

If in Christ Jesus we have become kings (Rev 1:6; 5:10), it is not fitting for us to become drunk with the wine of the love of this world and its pleasures, lest we forget the law of heaven and lose our fitting royal work, and demand the inner “Vashti” so that she may show her beauty before the peoples and the princes, that is, we present works of righteousness and virtues to gain human glory and for outward show, instead of our queen being within us, revealing her beauty only to her Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus!

If God has set man up as a spiritual king, then it is fitting for him not to demand his wife the queen in order to display her beauty, but to keep her in the house of the women, holding the feast for the women, so that they rejoice in her and submit to her. In other words, let our bodies (the wife) remain subject to the soul (the king), hidden in their royal conduct, living in a spirit of submission to the soul so as to remain holy in the Lord, sharing with the soul her glory and royal dignity. The Apostle Paul loved “Vashti,” that is, his royal body in the Lord, and left her in the house of the women, when he said: [I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway] (1 Cor 9:27), “For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church,” that is, as a king toward the queen. Let the soul know its leading position by the Holy Spirit, and let the body know its position as a helper to the soul and a partner with her in victory, and the whole man is deprived of the eternal royal glory.

The king wanted to bring out the beauty of the queen “for she was fair to look on,” and he did not realize that by displaying her beauty she loses her dignity and her image is disfigured. For this reason our Lord Jesus affirmed our obligation not to display our inner queen, when He says: “Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: that thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly” (Mt 6:3-4). Vashti remains in the house of the women when we offer worship to God not with the intent of appearing before people but by closing our inner doors and entering into the secret place, where we meet our unseen Bridegroom. As St. John Chrysostom says: [God Himself is unseen, therefore He wishes your prayer also to be unseen], and he also says: [God desires that the doors of the mind be shut rather than the (visible) doors].

entries.section: 3. Taking the kingdom away from Vashti:

paragraphs.text: 13 Then the king said to the wise men, which knew the times, (for so was the king’s manner toward all that knew law and judgment: 14 And the next unto him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king’s face, and which sat the first in the kingdom;) 15 “What shall we do unto the queen Vashti according to law, because she hath not performed the commandment of the king Ahasuerus by the chamberlains?” 16 And Memucan answered before the king and the princes, “Vashti the queen hath not done wrong to the king only, but also to all the princes, and to all the people that are in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus. 17 For this deed of the queen shall come abroad unto all women, so that they shall despise their husbands in their eyes, when it shall be reported, The king Ahasuerus commanded Vashti the queen to be brought in before him, but she came not. 18 Likewise shall the ladies of Persia and Media say this day unto all the king’s princes, which have heard of the deed of the queen. Thus shall there arise too much contempt and wrath. 19 If it please the king, let there go a royal commandment from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that it be not altered, That Vashti come no more before king Ahasuerus; and let the king give her royal estate unto another that is better than she. 20 And when the king’s decree which he shall make shall be published throughout all his empire, (for it is great,) all the wives shall give to their husbands honour, both to great and small.” 21 And the saying pleased the king and the princes; and the king did according to the word of Memucan: 22 For he sent letters into all the king’s provinces, into every province according to the writing thereof, and to every people after their language, that every man should bear rule in his own house, and that it should be published according to the language of every people.

When the queen refused to come, “the king was very wroth, and his anger burned in him” [12], and thus he turned to the opposite, from intense love and admiration for his wife the queen to flames of anger burning in him against her.

The king consulted the wise men who knew the times (perhaps meaning magicians and diviners) [13], and those who knew law and judgment... And since there seem to have been differences between the queen and Memucan, one of these counselors of the king, he exaggerated the matter and counted what Vashti had done as a wrong not only against the king and the princes but against all the men of his kingdom, for when the women hear what happened they will despise their husbands. And he asked that the kingdom be taken away from her and given to one who is better than she [19].

Memucan counted Vashti’s conduct as a breach of the law of nature and the law of the family, whereby the man loses his authority over his wife and the wife despises her husband, and he thought that it is laws that support the man and give him authority. Perhaps this conduct reveals an inner feeling that was passing through the lives of men in that age, namely the inability to control and lead the family; they did not realize that wise leadership does not draw its strength from laws and commands but from a spirit of self-giving love, as the Apostle says: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it... Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself” (Eph 5:25, 33).

entries.section: 3. Taking the kingdom away from Vashti:

paragraphs.text: Memucan says: “that every man should bear rule in his own house, and that it should be published according to the language of every people” [22], meaning that if a man marries a woman of another race, the household is obliged to speak the language of the man and not the woman. This is the picture of family life in the minds of the men of Persia, and they did not realize that the language that prevails in the home must be the language of love, which is able to captivate the beloved. Between wife and husband there is no struggle for authority; rather there ought to be between them a longing for self-giving that works through inner love, and an awareness of the unity of life and thought.

Ahasuerus loved Vashti for her beauty, her lineage and her wealth, and in his anger he took counsel with others about her. We, however, receive the wife (or the husband) from the hand of God, that He may grant us the spirit of unity in Him, sanctifying the family relationship which cannot be dissolved. As Tertullian says: [How can I describe the happiness of the marriage that the Church approves, the offering confirms, the blessing seals, the angels announce, and the Father declares lawful?!].

entries.section: 1. The need for a new queen:

paragraphs.text: 1 After these things, when the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her. 2 Then said the king’s servants that ministered unto him, “Let there be fair young virgins sought for the king: 3 And let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together all the fair young virgins unto Shushan the palace, to the house of the women, unto the custody of Hege the king’s chamberlain, keeper of the women; and let their things for purification be given them: 4 And let the maiden which pleaseth the king be queen instead of Vashti.” And the thing pleased the king; and he did so.

“After these things, when the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her. Then said the king’s servants that ministered unto him, Let there be fair young virgins sought for the king: and let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together all the fair young virgins unto Shushan the palace, to the house of the women, unto the custody of Hege the king’s chamberlain, keeper of the women; and let their things for purification be given them: and let the maiden which pleaseth the king be queen instead of Vashti” [1-3].

The king’s wrath was appeased and he remembered Vashti, and perhaps he could have pardoned her, but the counselors feared lest she take vengeance on them because of their counsel to the king, so they hastened to urge him to choose a beautiful wife. It is said that the king used to choose his wife from the daughters of the princes, but since the men feared that the king would think they had pushed him to dismiss Vashti for a personal interest, they tried to show their good intention by having the king choose the beautiful maiden from any province or any race, as they would gather for him the fair maidens from the whole kingdom. By this they wanted to offer a remedy for the dismissal of Vashti by installing a beautiful woman in her place. As St. Jerome says: [The philosophers of the world used to remove an old passion by instilling a new passion, driving out one nail by fixing another. On this basis the seven princes of Persia acted with King Ahasuerus, for they removed his regret over Vashti the queen by stirring up in him love for other virgins. They heal one fault with another, and one sin with another sin; but for us it is fitting to overcome our faults by teaching ourselves the love of the opposite virtues. As the psalmist says: “Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it” (Ps 34:14). For if we do not hate evil we cannot love good; rather let us do good if we wish to leave evil; let us seek peace if we wish to avoid war.]

The princes exploited the weakness of the king’s character and his love of licentiousness, so they quenched his longing for Vashti by offering beautiful maidens to the house of the women, that he might choose according to his desire.

If we take the symbolic or spiritual interpretation, we ask: who are these servants who minister to him and ask him to set up a new queen instead of Vashti, if not the men of faith of the Old Testament, patriarchs, prophets, kings, priests and laymen, who lived under the shadow of the Law (Vashti), and realized that there is no salvation for them by the Law, especially in its literalness, since “the commandment (the Law), which was ordained to life, I found to be unto death. For sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me” (Rom 7:10-11). The Law exposed sin and disgraced it (Rom 7:12) and confirmed the death of man instead of supporting, healing and saving him. For this reason the men of the Old Testament awaited with joy the coming of the “Messiah,” the Savior, to set up Esther as queen through the free grace of the Gospel, as the Lord Himself says: “Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad” (Jn 8:56).

The servants asked that the fair young virgins be gathered from the whole kingdom to Shushan the palace, as if they, the men of the Old Testament, saw the Church of the New Testament, which has included in its membership children from all the nations and peoples, and has entered with them into the house of the virgins in the palace of Christ, that is, the Church which is called “the church of the firstborn” (Heb 12:23), to declare her spiritual virginity and her inner beauty as “a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish” (Eph 5:27). The believers longed to see this holy virgin as a bride for the King, as the Apostle Paul says: “For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor 11:2).

5 Now in Shushan the palace there was a certain Jew, whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite; 6 Who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity which had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away. 7 And he brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle’s daughter: for she had neither father nor mother, and the maid was fair and beautiful; whom Mordecai, when her father and mother were dead, took for his own daughter. 8 So it came to pass, when the king’s commandment and his decree was heard, and when many maidens were gathered together unto Shushan the palace, to the custody of Hegai, that Esther was brought also unto the king’s house, to the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women. 9 And the maiden pleased him, and she obtained kindness of him; and he speedily gave her her things for purification, with such things as belonged to her, and seven maidens, which were meet to be given her, out of the king’s house: and he preferred her and her maids unto the best place of the house of the women. 10 Esther had not shewed her people nor her kindred: for Mordecai had charged her that she should not shew it. 11 And Mordecai walked every day before the court of the women’s house, to know how Esther did, and what should become of her.

When Vashti was removed from the kingdom, God turned this matter to the salvation of His people by raising up Esther, who was born in the land of captivity and was brought up by her cousin Mordecai, as queen instead of Vashti.

The book speaks of Mordecai, who worked in Shushan the palace; he was a Jew carried away from Jerusalem in the days of Jeconiah king of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. What draws our attention is that the hidden hero in the story of Esther is “Mordecai,” who was marked by faithfulness in raising Esther and in his guidance to her, and by faithfulness in his work for the king, who was of a foreign race, saving his life from a wicked plot; he was also distinguished by a deeply spiritual conduct filled with faith and trust in the work of God.

We have said that Vashti signifies the literalness of the Law, which must be removed from the heart so that the grace of the New Testament may reign, and Esther (the Church of the New Testament) appears as queen. The features and circumstances of Esther came in conformity with the Church of the New Testament in many respects, of which we mention:

First: Esther was born in the land of captivity, deprived of the Promised Land and of the Temple with all its beautiful rituals, as if she represents the company of the Gentiles who fell under the captivity of the devil, deprived of God’s spiritual blessings and of the enjoyment of His temple... But God raised them from this captivity and made them spiritual kings, for the Lord Christ came to set them free, as it is said by Isaiah: “He hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound” (Isa 61:1).

St. Augustine says: [Our captivity was removed, not by our being freed from the hands of the barbarians... but from our evil works and from our sins by which the devil had dominion over us; whoever is freed from his sins, the chief of sinners (the devil) no longer has dominion over him], and he also says: [Confess that you are a captive and you will deserve to be freed; for he who does not know his enemy, how can he urge on his deliverer?].

Second: “she had neither father nor mother” [7], that is, she was an orphan. This is the mark of the Church when she fulfilled God’s call to Abraham: “Get thee... from thy father’s house” (Gen 12:1). Let us leave our old father, the devil, and our first mother, that is, the love of the world, so that the Lord Himself may be our heavenly Father and the heavenly Church our mother. The Lord asked the Jews to become orphans of their evil father when He said to them: “Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do” (Jn 8:44). And St. Augustine speaks about the Gentiles’ leaving their old father, saying: [The Gentiles came from their father Satan and renounced their sonship to him].

Third: “the maid was fair and beautiful” [7]... The heavenly Bridegroom sees in His bride the queen a beauty that He Himself poured upon her, for He says to her: “And thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD” (Ezek 16:14). Though our past was disgraced by the blackness of sin, yet with exultation we say: “I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1:5). And as St. Ambrose says: [Since you put on those garments through the font of Baptism, you say in the Song of Songs, “I am black, but comely (perfect), O ye daughters of Jerusalem.” I am black through human weakness, perfect through the mystery of faith].
Fourth: “(Hegai) moved her with her maids to the best place in the house of the women, and Esther did not tell of her people and her kindred” [9-10].

Hegai was the keeper of the house of the virgins, and Shaashgaz the keeper of the concubines [14]. As for Esther, she entered the house of the virgins and was placed in the best place in it, for he realized that she would find favour in the sight of the king and be made queen. What is this place if not “sonship to God,” which became ours as the gift of the Holy Spirit to us in Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son? For in Him we have been raised into the bosom of His Father, to be found with Him as sons of His.

Esther did not tell of her people and her kindred, as Mordecai counseled. For the soul, when it enjoys sonship to God and becomes a queen, lives on a heavenly level, and it has a transcendent race that language cannot express. She lives in silence, not the silence of helplessness grounded in the closing of the heart, but the silence of love opened toward heaven, contemplating the works of God with a glorious joy that cannot be spoken.

Fifth: her humility. Esther was marked by a spirit of obedience and submission to her foster father Mordecai even after she sat as queen on the greatest throne of that time, for it is said: “for Esther did the commandment of Mordecai, like as when she was brought up with him” [20].

12 Now when every maid’s turn was come to go in to king Ahasuerus, after that she had been twelve months, according to the manner of the women, (for so were the days of their purifications accomplished, to wit, six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet odours, and with other things for the purifying of the women;) 13 Then thus came every maiden unto the king; whatsoever she desired was given her to go with her out of the house of the women unto the king’s house. 14 In the evening she went, and on the morrow she returned into the second house of the women, to the custody of Shaashgaz, the king’s chamberlain, which kept the concubines: she came in unto the king no more, except the king delighted in her, and that she were called by name. 15 Now when the turn of Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her for his daughter, was come to go in unto the king, she required nothing but what Hegai the king’s chamberlain, the keeper of the women, appointed. And Esther obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her. 16 So Esther was taken unto king Ahasuerus into his house royal in the tenth month, which is the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign. 17 And the king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and favour in his sight more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti. 18 Then the king made a great feast unto all his princes and his servants, even Esther’s feast; and he made a release to the provinces, and gave gifts, according to the state of the king. 19 And when the virgins were gathered together the second time, then Mordecai sat in the king’s gate. 20 Esther had not yet shewed her kindred nor her people; as Mordecai had charged her: for Esther did the commandment of Mordecai, like as when she was brought up with him.

When Xerxes returned defeated from his campaign against Greece, he busied himself with choosing the new queen, and it seems that what was done by way of preparations with the virgins took place before his coming from the battle and not after his coming, since the virgins remained a whole year preparing for the meeting with the king. And the book relates to us the preparations that were made for Esther, which are:

First: the days of her purification were completed, “six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet odours, and with other things for the purifying of the women” [12]. What do the six months in which she was perfumed with oil of myrrh mean if not her acceptance of burial with her Bridegroom Christ, who was buried after being anointed with myrrh... She remains six months, and the number 6 signifies the days of creation, that is, she remains bearing sufferings and being buried with her Bridegroom all the days of her sojourn until her spiritual perfection is completed and she meets the Lord face to face on the seventh day. And as she is buried with the Lord, so she rises with Him, for the sweet odours and the ointments signify the joyous fragrance of the resurrection. Therefore let us suffer with Him, be buried with Him, and also rise with Him! This is the way to reach the heavenly crown. As St. John Chrysostom says: [It is fitting for you that these sufferings not trouble you but rather rejoice you... Thus it is fitting for us to walk the way so that we may share with Him in glory and honor... How glorious are the sufferings! By them we are conformed to His death!].

Second: “whatsoever she desired was given her to go with her out of the house of the women unto the king’s house” [13]. The virgin carries with her all that she wants from the house of the women (the virgins), for as she sets out to her Bridegroom the heavenly King, she carries what she has gathered here of holy things such as love, purity and heavenly thought. She carries it as a sign of love for her Bridegroom, from what He Himself gave her during the days of her sojourn on earth, that is, she offers to Him from what He gave her.

Third: “Esther obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her” [15]. This is her true asset: the free grace of God, which raises the soul and lifts her until she is fit for a kingdom (Ezek 16:13), so that she finds favour in the eyes of all... This is the grace of God that upholds man in his striving, of which St. John Chrysostom said: [None is stronger than he who enjoys heavenly help, as none is weaker than he who is deprived of it].

Fourth: “Esther was taken... in the tenth month, which is the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign” [16]. Esther could be set up as queen only in the tenth month in the seventh year. The tenth month signifies the fulfillment of the Law (10 commandments), which is accomplished through our union in Christ, who alone did not break the Law, while the seventh year signifies the perfection of the Gospel. It is as though our enjoyment of the Kingdom is realized by our receiving the Law spiritually in the Lord through the grace of the Gospel.

Fifth: “Then the king made a great feast unto all his princes and his servants, even Esther’s feast; and he made a release to the provinces, and gave gifts, according to the state of the king” [18]. Esther made him forget the troubles of his battle with Greece and his heavy loss, and his life was turned into joy, as he gave rest to the land, that is, exemption from tribute for a year or exemption from conscription...

The king put the crown with his own hands on her head [17], for the soul cannot reign except through Christ Jesus, who crowns her with the crown of His glory, and makes a feast in her name that gladdens the heart of the heavenly ones. And it is a rest, for the Lord counts her crown a blessed Sabbath and a joyous feast. As for His gifts, which are according to the king’s generosity, they are the giving of Himself to us as a Bridegroom whom we carry within us. He is the Giver and the gift; He does not withhold Himself from us but with joy receives us, that we may say: “My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies” (Song 2:16). And as St. Augustine addresses Him, saying: [You watch over me, as though You had forgotten all creation! You give me Your gifts, as if I alone were the object of Your love].

21 In those days, while Mordecai sat in the king’s gate, two of the king’s chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, of those which kept the door, were wroth, and sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus. 22 And the thing was known to Mordecai, who told it unto Esther the queen; and Esther certified the king thereof in Mordecai’s name. 23 And when inquisition was made of the matter, it was found out; therefore they were both hanged on a tree: and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king.
Mordecai was marked by faithfulness. He was faithful in his private life, as in his raising of Esther, and in his service to the king, as in his love for his people.

Mordecai learned that two chamberlains, keepers of the door, were plotting to assassinate the king, so he told Esther, who told the king. And when the king examined the matter and verified it, he hanged them on a tree, and the matter was written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of the Persians.

In (the Additions to Esth 12:4-5) it relates to us that the king gave gifts to Mordecai, but afterwards, when sleep fled from the king and he read what had been written earlier, he counted what Mordecai had received as nothing (Esth 6:1-11), and wanted to honor him in an extraordinary way. We also, when we strive here for the salvation of our brethren from eternal punishment, the Lord counts it as a debt, although He is the One working in us and with us, and so grants us blessings and graces; but all this He counts as nothing when He crowns us with the crown of eternal life and brings us into the fellowship of His glories, to live with Him face to face in the bosom of the Father.

1 After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him. 2 And all the king’s servants, that were in the king’s gate, bowed, and reverenced Haman: for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence. 3 Then the king’s servants, which were in the king’s gate, said unto Mordecai, “Why transgressest thou the king’s commandment?” 4 Now it came to pass, when they spake daily unto him, and he hearkened not unto them, that they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai’s matters would stand: for he had told them that he was a Jew. 5 And when Haman saw that Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence, then was Haman full of wrath. 6 And he thought scorn to lay hands on Mordecai alone; for they had shewed him the people of Mordecai: wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus, even the people of Mordecai.

“Haman” is the name of one of the chief gods in Elam, which the kingdom of Media and Persia took possession of and made one of its states, and it made its capital “Shushan” or “Susa” a capital where the kings of Persia stayed in the winter.

Haman the Agagite came from the descendants of Amalek (1 Sam 15:3, 9), whom Saul treated lightly and did not utterly destroy, so there came from them one who almost exterminated the whole people in one day. Thus Haman represents the sin that man makes light of and is careless in uprooting, so that his whole life is exposed to danger at the opportune moment.

“After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him. And all the king’s servants, that were in the king’s gate, bowed, and reverenced Haman” [1-2].

Haman had received great honor above all, so he became great in his own eyes, and wanted everyone to submit to him and bow down in worship of him. It is as though he bears the spirit of his master, the devil, who wanted to set himself up as a god. Therefore when Mordecai the Jew refused to bow to him [2], “Haman was full of wrath” [5], “and he thought scorn to lay hands on Mordecai alone; for they had shewed him the people of Mordecai: wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus, even the people of Mordecai” [6].

It is true that the Jews were accustomed to bow down before their kings as a mark of honor (2 Sam 14:4; 18:28; 1 Kgs 1:16), but the Persians offered worship to their kings, so the believers refused to take part with them in this act. And when Mordecai was asked about his not bowing down, “he had told them that he was a Jew” [4], and it was not permitted for him to take part with them in this act.

It is not strange that Haman should demand the extermination of all the people, for since he represents the devil while Mordecai is a type of the Lord Christ, the enemy of good cannot bear the people of Christ, who are the Kingdom of God.

Here we pause a little to see Mordecai as a type of the Lord Christ, because of whom Haman (the devil) wanted to exterminate all His people. Father Aphrahat says that just as Mordecai was persecuted by wicked Haman, so the wicked people persecuted the Lord Christ. And as Mordecai prayed for his people to save them from Haman, the Lord Christ intercedes for His people (by His blood) to save them from the devil. And as Mordecai was saved from his persecutor, the persecutors were unable to triumph over the Lord Christ. And as Mordecai sat in sackcloth and rescued his people, so the Word of God came down and took our body as in sackcloth and in humility saved us. Through Mordecai Esther became pleasing to the king instead of Vashti, and through Christ Jesus the Church of the New Testament became the object of the Father’s pleasure instead of the Jewish synagogue. And as Mordecai urged Esther to fast with her maidens, so the Lord Christ urges His Church with all her children to fast. Finally Mordecai received Haman’s glory, and it was proclaimed before him: [Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour] (Esth 6:11); and as for Jesus Christ, He was glorified with the glory that was His from eternity, and the guards bore witness to Him: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Mt 27:54).

Haman discovered that what Mordecai was doing was not based on personal enmity but on a spiritual foundation of piety, so he thought there was no remedy for this problem except the extermination of the whole people.

St. Jerome sees that the word “Haman” means (unjustly). Now when the flames of injustice are kindled into wrath, they only burn themselves, for he says: [Haman, which means (unjustly), was burned with the fire that he himself kindled].

Here it is fitting for us to affirm that what Mordecai did in not bowing down to Haman was not out of hatred or enmity within his heart, nor out of pride, but as he said in his prayer found in the Additions to Esther: “Thou knowest all things, and knowest that it was not out of pride, nor contempt, nor desire for any honor that I did this, that I did not bow down to the arrogant Haman. For I am ready to kiss even the traces of his feet with a willing mind for the deliverance of Israel, but I feared to turn the honor of my God to a man and to worship anyone but my God” (Additions to Esth 13:12-14).
He does not disdain to kiss the traces of Haman’s feet for the salvation of his brethren; thus his heart is enlarged with love and filled with humility, but he does not accept to worship any but God!

7 In the first month, that is, the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of king Ahasuerus, they cast Pur, that is, the lot, before Haman from day to day, and from month to month, to the twelfth month, that is, the month Adar. 8 And Haman said unto king Ahasuerus, “There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the people in all the provinces of thy kingdom; and their laws are diverse from all people; neither keep they the king’s laws: therefore it is not fitting for the king to suffer them. 9 If it please the king, let it be written that they may be destroyed: and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver to the hands of those that have the charge of the business, to bring it into the king’s treasuries.” 10 And the king took his ring from his hand, and gave it unto Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the Jews’ enemy. 11 And the king said unto Haman, “The silver is given to thee, the people also, to do with them as it seemeth good to thee.” 12 Then were the king’s scribes called on the thirteenth day of the first month, and there was written according to all that Haman had commanded unto the king’s lieutenants, and to the governors that were over every province, and to the rulers of every people of every province according to the writing thereof, and to every people after their language; in the name of king Ahasuerus was it written, and sealed with the king’s ring. 13 And the letters were sent by posts into all the king’s provinces, to destroy, to kill, and to cause to perish, all Jews, both young and old, little children and women, in one day, even upon the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, and to take the spoil of them for a prey. 14 The copy of the writing for a commandment to be given in every province was published unto all people, that they should be ready against that day.

Since Haman counted the insult that came to him from Mordecai as not atoned for by the killing of one person, he demanded the extermination of the whole Jewish people. So in April of the year 474 B.C., that is, about 4 years after Esther’s coronation, Haman asked the diviners and magicians to cast Pur, that is, a lot, so as to determine the proper day for exterminating this people so that his plan would not fail. They fixed it on the thirteenth day of the last month of the year (the month of Adar), and thus gave him a long and sufficient respite to accomplish his purpose in one day in all parts of the kingdom.

Haman met the king and incited him against the people by accusing them of being breakers of the laws who deserve nothing but extermination, and he offered ten thousand talents of silver as the price of this work. As we have said, he wanted to gather the wealth of all the Jews, so that he would become rich and offer this sum to the king, perhaps to compensate him for his losses a few years earlier in his war against Greece, or in return for his losses of the tribute that the Jews used to pay. For the Jews were known for exaggerated wealth even in the land of captivity; in recent discoveries many Jewish names have been found performing the work of money-changers in the region of Babylon in the period of the captivity.

The king handed his ring to Haman, and said to him: “The silver... is given to thee, the people also, to do with them as it seemeth good to thee” [11]. Thus the king trusted Haman and loved him so much that he handed him the ring to write what he wished; even the silver that Haman offered to give the king as compensation he waived to him, and as for the whole people, they were in his hands to do with as he wished... And indeed “the letters were sent by posts into all the king’s provinces, to destroy, to kill, and to cause to perish, all Jews, both young and old, little children and women, in one day, even upon the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, and to take the spoil of them for a prey” [13]. It is a faint picture of the sentence that was passed on us because of the envy of Haman (the devil), so that all without exception came under the sentence of death, so that everyone who looks at himself makes great mourning and weeps day and night (Esth 4:3). And as the Apostle says: “Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men” (Rom 5:12).

This bitter sentence turns against Haman and his followers through Mordecai and Esther and becomes salvation, joy and a feast for all the people. Thus if through the devil we fell under the sentence of death, then through Christ Jesus (the true Mordecai) Esther and her people (the Church) enjoyed salvation, joy and the heavenly feast, while the devil and all his soldiers collapsed beneath the Cross. As the Apostle says: “Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross; and having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Col 2:14-15).

entries.section: 3. The king and Haman sit down to drink:

paragraphs.text: 15 The posts went out, being hastened by the king’s commandment, and the decree was given in Shushan the palace. And the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed.

The king had only one ear, with which he listened to Haman without inquiring about the other side. He did not examine the matter himself but handed everything over into Haman’s hand. And since Haman feared lest the king retract and realize the matter, he drank with him, so that the king would be distracted by his pleasures at the expense of his people.

The “Additions to Esther” found in the Septuagint present to us a copy of the royal decree sent in the name of Ahasuerus, addressed to all the states or the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces, and it agreed with the conversation mentioned in this chapter between Haman and the king. The most important of what it contained:

First: the Jews were accused of ingratitude, as people to whom the king does good and who repay the kindness by violating the laws, and he considered that their destruction brings peace to all the lands, for he says: “so that when those wicked people go down to hell in one day, the peace which they disturbed may be restored to our kingdom” (Additions to Esth 13:7).

Second: Haman was called the second man after the king, and the king honors him as a father, so all are obliged to follow his counsel concerning the extermination of this enemy people, they and their wives and their children. Here we pause a little at the calling of Haman “a father,” for he represents the devil, who offers his followers an evil fatherhood, as the Lord Christ said to the wicked Jews: “Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do” (Jn 8:44). Just as God offers us His fatherhood, so that we bear as sons the characteristics of our Father and enjoy the fellowship of His eternal glory, so the enemy of good, the devil, offers his fatherhood to his followers that they may bear his characteristics and share his eternal destruction.

“1 When Mordecai perceived all that was done, Mordecai rent his clothes, and put on sackcloth with ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and cried with a loud and a bitter cry; 2 And came even before the king’s gate: for none might enter into the king’s gate clothed with sackcloth. 3 And in every province, whithersoever the king’s commandment and his decree came, there was great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and wailing; and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.” [1-3].

When Mordecai learned what Haman had done, he rent his clothes as a sign of intense grief, as Reuben did when he returned to the pit and did not find Joseph his brother (Gen 37:29), and he put on sackcloth as a sign of the contrition of his heart and his humbling, and cried with a bitter cry, for he realized that what had befallen his people was because of him... Moreover Mordecai enjoyed a heart enlarged with love for his brethren, so he could not bear to see their sufferings. He is like Nehemiah, who heard the grievous news in Jerusalem and said: “I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven” (Neh 1:4). And the Apostle Paul bore the same heart when he said: [I say the truth in Christ, I lie not, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost, That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart. For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh] (Rom 9:1-3).

If Mordecai represents the Lord Christ, then the way of salvation began with Mordecai’s rending his clothes, putting on sackcloth, and going out into the city to cry with a bitter cry that shakes the gates of heaven, so that Queen Esther and her people are saved from extermination. Thus the Lord Christ laid aside His glory, emptying Himself for our sake (the rending of the clothes), taking our body (putting on sackcloth), dwelling in our midst on our earth (his going out into the city), and cried on the Cross to give up His spirit for our salvation. As Father Aphrahat says: [When Mordecai sat and wrapped himself in sackcloth he rescued Esther and her people from the sword; since Christ put on a body... He saved the Church and her children from death].

In every province to which the king’s command came, the life of the Jews was turned into mourning, fasting and weeping, and many spread sackcloth, following the example of Mordecai... It is a living picture of the believers who contemplate the great Day of the Lord and, as they realize the work of sin within them, mourn, offering sincere repentance so as to seize the mercies of the Lord.

Finally Mordecai came before the king’s gate but did not enter because of the sackcloth. Thus the kings lived in their palaces, not wanting to meet the suffering and the wronged, caring for their own psychological comfort without concern for the people. They closed the doors before the one clothed in sackcloth, so that the King of kings Himself might come down clothed in sackcloth, and share their sufferings, and lead them by His Holy Spirit not to the king’s gate or inside his palace, but to the very bosom of the Father. Thus the great closed the doors of their palaces in the face of the needy, so that the Great One might come down to them and carry them to His heavens.

entries.section: 2. Esther’s grief and her sending Hatach to him:

paragraphs.text: 4 So Esther’s maids and her chamberlains came and told it her. Then was the queen exceedingly grieved; and she sent raiment to clothe Mordecai, and to take away his sackcloth from him: but he received it not. 5 Then called Esther for Hatach, one of the king’s chamberlains, whom he had appointed to attend upon her, and gave him a commandment to Mordecai, to know what it was, and why it was. 6 So Hatach went forth to Mordecai unto the street of the city, which was before the king’s gate. 7 And Mordecai told him of all that had happened unto him, and of the sum of the money that Haman had promised to pay to the king’s treasuries for the Jews, to destroy them. 8 Also he gave him the copy of the writing of the decree that was given at Shushan to destroy them, to shew it unto Esther, and to declare it unto her, and to charge her that she should go in unto the king, to make supplication unto him, and to make request before him for her people. 9 And Hatach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai.

Esther was exceedingly grieved when she heard what Mordecai had done, and she sent him garments, but he did not accept to take his sackcloth off him. So she sent to him Hatach, one of the chamberlains who were in her attendance, and Mordecai told him all that Haman had done and gave him a copy of the king’s decree, and asked him to charge Esther to go in unto the king, and make supplication unto him, and make request of him for her people.

If Mordecai put on sackcloth in humbling himself before God, then in courage he declared his grief in the midst of the city and did not hide the bitterness of his soul; when the queen asked him to put on garments that she sent to him, he refused. She sent him Hatach, who seems to have been a Jew, since it is said of him in the second Targum that he had another name, “Daniel.” For this reason Mordecai spoke to him with complete frankness and asked him to declare the matter to Esther, that she might intervene by meeting with the king.

10 Again Esther spake unto Hatach, and gave him commandment unto Mordecai; 11 “All the king’s servants, and the people of the king’s provinces, do know, that whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called, there is one law of his to put him to death, except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live: but I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days.” 12 And they told to Mordecai Esther’s words. 13 Then Mordecai commanded to answer Esther, “Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king’s house, more than all the Jews. 14 For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father’s house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” 15 Then Esther bade them return Mordecai this answer, 16 “Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.” 17 So Mordecai went his way, and did according to all that Esther had commanded him.

When Hatach told Esther the words of Mordecai, she sent to him saying that she had not been called to go in to the king these thirty days, and if she went in she would be killed unless the king held out the golden sceptre, and then she would live. But he returned to tell her: “Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king’s house, more than all the Jews. For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father’s house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” [13-14].

If Mordecai rent his clothes, put on sackcloth and cried with a bitter cry in the midst of the city, it was not out of despair or loss of hope but out of humbling himself before God, believing that He is able to act, and urging his people to share with him in contrition before God... This is what his words to Esther revealed, for he believed that salvation was surely coming, through Esther or through another, God works, for he says to her: “For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place.” It is as though he says to her: God does not lack the means; He will save in any case, but I fear that you will lose your crown, for perhaps He sent you to this place to work through you so that you may enjoy the crown.

Would that in the time of temptation we were like Mordecai, who believes that salvation is surely coming and that God will certainly rescue; yet would that we come out of the temptation conquerors and victorious, not broken and losers. If we believe in the work of God, the temptation ends and we have been crowned in His eyes, and we acquire for ourselves gain on a heavenly level.

Mordecai affirmed to Esther that the events of her life are not a collection of coincidences nor the fruit of purely human striving, but a divine plan for the glory of God, the building up of the Church and the growth of Esther’s spiritual life. So Joseph believed when he said to his brethren who had delivered him into slavery: “Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life” (Gen 45:5)... So if Esther has become queen or Joseph was sold as a slave, God, the Lord of history, brings them in to where they glorify Him on behalf of the whole holy community.

Mordecai revealed to her that she should come out of the circle of narrow thinking, and not think about her life or her death, because what befalls her people touches her life and the life of her father’s house, for he says to her: “Think not... that thou shalt escape in the king’s house.” At the same time he affirmed to her that the work she does is done by God Himself, for He will surely save; so if she stretches out her hand to the work, God Himself, as a Father, is committed to the work... so do not fear.
Would that we always work going forth from the circle of the ego, realizing that the spiritual work of God will not fail, and that His hand is able to save if we deliver our lives into His hands.

If Mordecai confronted Esther with frankness and courage to remove from her all fear, then in humility the queen received his message, and her answer revealed a heart enlarged with transcendent love, for she said: “Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish” [16].

Esther loved her people, so she offered her life to death for them: “if I perish, I perish.” Though she was a great queen, fair to look on, in the prime of her life, loved by her husband, she accepted to go in to him without his calling her, though she knew his savagery, which knows no mercy even toward his friends. For when Lysias begged him to spare his eldest son from the war, offering his other five sons, all he did was cut the boy in two and ask the soldiers to walk over his body with their feet, so that all would know his firmness and sternness.

She exposed her life to destruction by faith. She did not cast blame on Mordecai nor accuse him of pride for not submitting to Haman, but by a living faith realized that her own sins and those of all her people were the cause, for we hear in her prayer found in the Additions to Esther that she says: “And now we have sinned before thee, and thou hast delivered us into the hands of our enemies, because we worshipped their gods: O Lord, thou art righteous” (Additions to Esth 14:6-7)... By faith she knew the key of salvation: confession of sins and returning to God the Savior.

Esther did not think in a human, temporal way. She did not care how to adorn herself and perfume herself to attract the king, nor did she ask Mordecai to arrange a plot against Haman, but she knew that salvation is from God, so she resorted to fasting and prayer, and asked that Mordecai and all the other Jews who were in the city of Shushan (Susa) share with her, as her maids shared with her... And here we pause at her maids’ sharing with her in her fasting from eating and drinking three days and in her prayers, for in this is a revelation of Esther’s life with them. She lived with them not as one giving commands and prohibitions but as a mother caring for their salvation; they bore with her the spirit of piety and godliness, therefore they shared with her in her distress with fitting spiritual thought! Would that we cared even for servants, for we are responsible for their salvation as brethren to us who share with us membership in the one Body.

It was necessary for Esther to go in to the king, but she wanted to enter into his heart by God, in whose hand alone is the king’s heart (Prov 21:1). So she resorted to Him by fasting and prayer, that He might change his stony nature and open his doors to her, so that she would enter with the Lord Himself to save her with her people. In this St. Ambrose says: [Esther by her fasts moved the arrogant king]. And St. Clement of Rome says: [Esther, who was perfect in faith, exposed herself to a danger no less (than Judith), to rescue the twelve tribes of Israel from certain destruction. For she besought by fasting and humility the everlasting God who sees all things, and He, seeing the humility of her spirit, saved the people for whose sake she had exposed herself to death]. And it is stated in the book (the Constitutions of the Holy Apostles): “By fasting Esther, Mordecai and Judith escaped the plots of the wicked Holofernes and Haman.”

With perfect love for her people and perfect trust in God, who works in the lives of the humble, Esther fasted and went forth with courage to the work, saying: “if I perish, I perish,” not out of unbelief in God’s salvation, but out of love, ready to perish that the people might live, and to die for her brethren. And as St. Ambrose says: [Why did Esther expose her life to death and not fear the wrath of the savage king? Was it not to save her people from death, a fitting matter filled with virtue!].

Esther bore the spirit of the three youths who said: “If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not (even if we die bodily), be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Dan 3:17-18).

She asked for an absolute fast from all eating and drinking for three days, as though she wanted to enter with the Lord into His tomb in order to rise with Him on the third day. She believed in Him who is able to raise her and her people from death. It is as though she shared with Jonah, the type of Christ, and entered into the belly of the whale, beholding the burial of the Lord Christ and His bearing death for His people, in order to come forth preaching the good tidings of life.

It is stated in the Additions to Esther (Additions to Esth 14) that she took off the royal garments and put on garments of grief and weeping, and instead of the various perfumes she cast ashes on her head, and humbled her body with fasting, and she tore out the hair of her head, and stood supplicating God, confessing her sins and those of her people, reminding Him of His promises and His works with her fathers, and asking Him to look upon the humiliation of His people and their distress at the hands of the pagans.

Esther believed that it is God who speaks through her mouth so that the words would pierce the heart of this savage lion, for she said: “Put eloquent speech in my mouth before the lion, and turn his heart to hate our enemy, that there may be an end of him and of all that are likeminded to him.” (Additions to Esth 14:13). For she does not capture the king’s heart by her beauty or her coquetry or her own wisdom, but by God, who speaks in her mouth and works in the heart of this lion. St. John Chrysostom says: [Esther rescued the whole people of the Jews when it was about to perish utterly, by using this means (prayer)...! She asked the merciful God to go with her to the king, and offered Him her prayers, when she said: “Put in my mouth acceptable speech...”].

In her prayer Esther revealed her inner life. She lived as a great queen possessing glory and honor, yet her heart was exceedingly simple, nothing of the honor of this world and its pleasures entering it. As she said: “Thou knowest my necessity: that I abhor the sign of my high estate, which is upon mine head in the days wherein I shew myself, and that I abhor it as a menstruous rag, and that I wear it not when I am private by myself. And that thine handmaid hath not eaten at Haman’s table, and that I have not delighted in the king’s feast, nor drunk the wine of the drink offerings. Neither hath thine handmaid had any joy since the day that I was brought hither to this present, but in thee, O Lord God of Abraham” (Additions to Esth 14:16-18).

Thus she lived in the palace as a queen, but she realized that she was a captive woman; her crown in her eyes was like a menstruous rag, she did not desire it but found it burdensome. She did not eat with Haman, the second man after the king, nor did she find pleasure in the king’s table, nor did she share in drinking the wine offered as a libation to the gods, and none gladdened her except the God of Abraham!

And this explains to us how, when she went in to the king before her selection, “she required nothing but what Hegai the king’s chamberlain appointed” (Esth 2:15), since her heart was not attached to anything, even the crown of the kingdom!

St. Augustine presented Esther to us as an example for those who are in office and have high and great positions and are busy in public affairs, but whose hearts are open to heaven, for he says: [Of this kind is the holy lady Esther, who, although she was the king’s wife, exposed her life to danger interceding for her people; when she prayed, she said that the royal adornment was to her like a menstruous rag].

And when St. Jerome praised one of the women recently consecrated to the Lord, he said: [She came to hate every splendid garment, and cried out to the Lord like Esther: “Thou knowest my necessity, that I abhor the sign of my high estate and my glory (that is, the crown she wore as queen), and I abhor it as a menstruous rag”].

1 Now it came to pass on the third day, that Esther put on her royal apparel, and stood in the inner court of the king’s house, over against the king’s house: and the king sat upon his royal throne in the royal house, over against the gate of the house. 2 And it was so, when the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, that she obtained favour in his sight: and the king held out to Esther the golden sceptre that was in his hand. So Esther drew near, and touched the top of the sceptre.

“Now it came to pass on the third day, that Esther put on her royal apparel, and stood in the inner court of the king’s house, over against the king’s house: and the king sat upon his royal throne in the royal house, over against the gate of the house” [1].

Esther prepared herself for this meeting with fasting and humbling together with prayer, and came to meet the king on the third day to invite him with Haman to a feast that she was preparing for them. Many of the Fathers saw that the number “3” signifies the resurrection. If Esther’s feast signifies the feast of the Cross, which the Lord prepared to save His people and to crucify the devil and all his wicked works, then she went forth to this feast in the spirit of the resurrection. In other words, if this feast signifies the Cross, then the destruction that befell Haman is through the Cross of the Lord who rose from the dead. On the Cross the true Haman, that is, the devil, perished, because He who was lifted up on the Cross is “the Resurrection” Himself (Jn 11:25).

Esther went to the king as to the Cross through the power of the Lord’s resurrection; therefore she took off the sackcloth and put on royal garments, for she believed in God who raises the needy from the dunghill.

The Additions to Esther present to us a magnificent and detailed picture of Esther’s meeting with the king (Additions to Esth 15), mentioning that when she took off the garments of her mourning and put on the garments of her glory, she called upon the Governor of all and Savior of all, God [5]. It is as though she declares that for His sake she took off the sackcloth and for His sake she put on glory, and that she would not set out to the work without Him. She called upon Him to accompany her, indeed to be in her heart and speak on her tongue, indeed that she herself be hidden in Him so that He might shoot His arrows into the king’s heart to turn it from cruelty to love. She called upon God the Savior of all since she knew that “The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Prov 21:1).

Esther went with two maidservants, leaning on one as though she could not stand because of her delicateness and luxury, while the other followed her, bearing up her train... And she was radiant in color in the prime of her beauty, and her face was pleasant and very lovable. She passed through all the doors, door after door, and then stood before the king, where he was sitting on his throne in his royal attire, adorned with gold and jewels, and his appearance was terrible. He lifted up his eyes and showed the wrath of his heart by the blazing of his eyes, so the queen fell and the color of her face turned to pallor, and she leaned her head on the maidservant in faintness. But God changed the spirit of the king to gentleness, and he hastened and rose from the throne in concern and embraced her in his arms until she came to herself, and he comforted her with these words: “What is the matter, Esther? I am thy brother; be not afraid. Thou shalt not die, for the law is not for thee but for the common people. Come near and touch the sceptre.” And as she still was silent, he took the golden sceptre and laid it upon her neck and her heart, and said: “Why dost thou not speak to me?!” And she answered and said: “I saw thee, my lord, as an angel of God, and my heart was troubled for fear of thy glory. For wonderful art thou, lord, and thy countenance is full of grace.” And while she was speaking she fell again and almost fainted, and the king was troubled, and all his attendants comforted her.
It is a wonderful meeting that reveals the meeting of the living Church, hidden in Christ Jesus who rose from the dead, with the Father, that she may enjoy His love and His eternal embraces.

I say, how much we need to go forth with Esther on the third day, carrying within us the power of the Lord’s resurrection, which removes our mourning and gives us inner glories and royal garments fitting for our meeting with the heavenly Lord. Let us go forth with her, and let us also have two maidservants, leaning on the one while the other bears our train; as the Word of God took humanity as His maidservant and so appeared in the form of weakness though He is King of kings, but humanity, the other maidservant, remained behind, submitting to His divine work in harmony... Thus, with the difference, let us lean on the body as a maidservant that submits to our souls in the Lord, and let the body be behind us, walking in the steps of the Spirit and serving it, and not dominating it, moving it by its desires and temporal pleasures.

Let us walk with Esther, who appeared faint, as though she were falling under the Cross with her Christ, drinking with Him the cup of His sufferings and sharing the likeness of His death so as to bear the power of His resurrection.

Let us be like Esther, hidden in God our Savior, entering from door to door until she reaches the presence of the king. Thus the Word of God leads us in from strength to strength (Ps 84:7), and takes us from glory to glory (2 Cor 3:18), and the everlasting doors are opened before us for His sake (Ps 24:7).

Finally, when she went in to the king, he comforted her: “Esther, I am thy brother; be not afraid. Thou shalt not die, for the law is not for thee but for the common people.” Do we not hear the same words when we enter the bosom of the Father and find the Son a firstborn brother to us, interceding for us that we may enjoy fellowship in His glories, so that we do not fear judgment, for we shall not die? As the Apostle Paul says boldly: “Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us” (Rom 8:32-34).

The king embraced Esther in his arms and put the golden sceptre on her neck; thus the Father embraces us in His bosom and sets us up as a queen by the Cross (the golden sceptre), which we have received, carrying it with the Lord on our necks.

As for her saying that she saw him as an angel of God and her heart was troubled by the awe of his glory, it carries a symbol of the Church, who beholds the mysteries of God and sees His face and enters into the ecstasy of an eternal love that never ceases, and remains through all her eternity contemplating Him with love mingled with awe!

Now we repeat what St. Augustine said: [Did not God accomplish for her what she asked of Him (Additions to Esth 14:13), for He worked in the king’s heart... He heard her, and changed his heart by a hidden, effective power even before he heard her entreaties].

entries.section: 2. Inviting the king and Haman to the feast:

paragraphs.text: 3 Then said the king unto her, “What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what is thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom.” 4 And Esther answered, “If it seem good unto the king, let the king and Haman come this day unto the banquet that I have prepared for him.” 5 Then the king said, “Cause Haman to make haste, that he may do as Esther hath said.” So the king and Haman came to the banquet that Esther had prepared. 6 And the king said unto Esther at the banquet of wine, “What is thy petition? and it shall be granted thee: and what is thy request? even to the half of the kingdom it shall be performed.” 7 Then answered Esther, and said, “My petition and my request is; 8 If I have found favour in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my petition, and to perform my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare for them, and I will do to morrow as the king hath said.”

The historian Herodotus says that the kings of Media used to refuse to let anyone enter the throne room unless he was summoned, to display their majesty and awe and at the same time to protect themselves from any assassination. As for Esther, she did not merely enter to where the throne was, but entered into the heart of the king, who embraced her in his arms and began to comfort her and ask her: “What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what is thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom!” [3]. The king did not expect Esther’s answer: “My petition and my request is; if I have found favour in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my petition, and to perform my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare for them, and I will do to morrow as the king hath said” [7-8].

entries.section: 2. Inviting the king and Haman to the feast:

paragraphs.text: We do not know why Esther postponed her request at a time when the king promised her that he would give her even up to half the kingdom. Did she feel some fear and want to gather her courage by prayer throughout the day? Or perhaps in her wisdom she did not want to hasten the request lest the king feel that she had pressed him and exploited his love for her?! But we know a more important explanation: she had to postpone the talk until the next day so that the cup of Haman’s wickedness might be filled and he might make the cross for Mordecai [14] so that he himself would be crucified on it. The hand of God pushed her to postpone so that God’s saving plan might be accomplished in its most wonderful form: Mordecai is glorified by Haman’s humiliation, as it was proclaimed before him in the square of the city: “Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour” (Esth 6:11), and Haman prepares the gallows for himself.

The postponement of the request was apparently by a divine revelation, if not in a tangible form then by God’s work in her heart and on her tongue, as she herself asked that He give her words of wisdom... And during this postponement God hastened to glorify Mordecai after God took sleep from the king’s eyes (Esth 6), and Haman hastened to kindle the fire to burn himself.

As for why she asked Haman to be present with the king, and this was the first time that she asked him to eat with them, as appears from Haman’s own joy and his saying to his family and friends: “Yea, Esther the queen did let no man come in with the king unto the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and to morrow am I invited unto her also with the king” [12], perhaps it is because, since she wanted to complain of him to the king, she did not accept to do so behind his back, but face to face with him. She wanted to strike two birds with one stone: to please the king by the coming of Haman, who was much beloved to him, and at the same time to accuse Haman before the king in his presence.

In any case, if this feast is the feast of the Cross that the Church holds at Golgotha, it is only to invite the King, that He may rejoice in the fruit of His suffering Church risen from the dead, and Haman attends to be condemned to the Cross and lose all his power. As St. Jerome says: [On the Cross Christ was lifted up crucified according to the flesh, but He crucified the devil and shattered his authority.

9 Then went Haman forth that day joyful and with a glad heart: but when Haman saw Mordecai in the king’s gate, that he stood not up, nor moved for him, he was full of indignation against Mordecai. 10 Nevertheless Haman refrained himself: and when he came home, he sent and called for his friends, and Zeresh his wife. 11 And Haman told them of the glory of his riches, and the multitude of his children, and all the things wherein the king had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes and servants of the king. 12 Haman said moreover, “Yea, Esther the queen did let no man come in with the king unto the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and to morrow am I invited unto her also with the king. 13 Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.” 14 Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, “Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet.” And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made.

“Then went Haman forth that day joyful and with a glad heart” [9], for this proud man, who thinks only of himself, counted that the queen desired to honor him by his accompanying the king at the feast, and did not know that she had invited him for his condemnation, like those who are self-admiring, deceiving themselves, as it was said to Edom: “Thou art greatly despised. The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee” (Obad 1:2-3).

He went out joyful and with a glad heart, but his joy lasted only moments, for at the gate before leaving the palace he saw Mordecai not bowing down to him, and he was filled with indignation... And so Haman gathered his household and his friends to declare to them his wealth and honor, saying: “Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate” [13]. He cannot bear to see Mordecai sitting at the king’s gate even if he himself is invited to the king’s feast. This is the mind of the devil toward the children of God, for he cannot bear any of them to sit at the gate of the King of kings, counting this a loss to him.

Let us contemplate the person of Mordecai, who offered fasts and humbling and cried bitterly in the midst of the city; we find him returning to the palace after the period of humbling, and not bowing down in prostration to Haman, for he does not accept to appease a man at the expense of the truth, nor to offer to a man what is fitting for God alone.

And since Haman had lost his peace, his wife and all his friends advised him to make a gallows fifty cubits high so that in the morning he might ask for the crucifixion of Mordecai before going in to the feast, and Haman made the gallows.

Haman made the gallows as the devil prepared the Cross through his helpers, and when Haman thought that he was crucifying Mordecai, he himself was crucified on it. So also when the devil counted that he would be rid of the Lord Christ by the Cross, the devil himself is crucified secretly, losing his authority over the Lord’s believers (Col 2:14-15).

He made a cross whose height was 50 cubits so that he might enjoy seeing Mordecai crucified while he was in the palace, from afar, and so slake his thirst for revenge. But the number 50 carries a symbolic meaning, for it signifies freedom, since in the Jubilee (the fiftieth year) the Jews granted slaves liberty, and the land was set free and returned to its owners... And by the Cross believing humanity was set free from the true Haman. For on the Cross it sees its Christ opening His arms to embrace the whole world, Jews and Gentiles, to set them free from the captivity of the devil and take them to the bosom of His Father.

entries.section: 1. The king recalls the deeds of Mordecai:
